snippet.title: Why the World Keeps Getting Trapped at Hormuz 😳🤔
snippet.description:
In July 1987, an oil tanker struck a mine in the Persian Gulf. Then something unexpected happened: the warships escorting it fell in behind the damaged tanker.

Why did this narrow sea route become so important to the world?

🌍 The Strait of Hormuz is more than a line on a map. It connects the Persian Gulf to the wider ocean, linking energy producers, refineries, shipping routes, and customers across the globe.

In this illustrated historical documentary, we uncover the story behind one of the world's most important maritime chokepoints.

⚓️ Inside this documentary:
- The strange 1987 incident that changed a naval convoy's formation
- The trading kingdom of Hormuz and the Portuguese fortress
- How oil discovered in Persia became connected to global shipping
- Iran's struggle over oil and sovereignty
- The Iran–Iraq War and the Tanker War
- Why millions of barrels of oil pass through this narrow route
- What recent shipping incidents reveal about the risks of maritime trade
- Why alternative pipelines cannot replace every shipment

📜 From historic trading ships to modern oil tankers, the vessels have changed — but the geography remains.

snippet.title: Did the Dog Really Find the Stolen World Cup Trophy?! 😱🏆 12 Fake (But Are True) Football Stories
snippet.description:
A dog found a stolen World Cup trophy. A coin toss sent a team to a European final. A World Cup final hat-trick still ended in defeat.

These sound made up. They're part of football history.

Explore 12 true football stories through illustrated stickman storytelling, from Pickles and the strange rules of early football to Liverpool's Istanbul comeback, goal-line technology, and Argentina vs France in 2022.

Along the way, discover the goalkeeper who proposed penalties, the traffic lights behind yellow and red cards, the barriers faced by women's football, Uruguay's 1950 upset, the Disgrace of Gijon, and the back-pass rule that changed goalkeeping.

Which story was hardest to believe? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for more illustrated football history.

Visuals are stylized reconstructions of historical events.

snippet.title: Did Ancient People Play Football? The Ball Is Only Half the Story
snippet.description:
Did ancient people really play football?

Thousands of years before modern association football, people were already playing games with balls. But does that mean football is thousands of years old?

In this documentary, we follow three kinds of historical evidence: surviving objects, images of people playing, and written rules. From the leather balls found near Yanghai in ancient China, to rubber balls from Mesoamerica, cuju in China, kemari in Japan, and the formation of the Football Association in England in 1863, we explore what the evidence actually tells us. 

You'll discover:

⚽️ Ancient leather balls found near Yanghai
🟤 Rubber ball technology in Mesoamerica
🦵 Why some Mesoamerican ballgames used the hips instead of the feet
🇨🇳 The ancient Chinese game of cuju
🇯🇵 The cooperative Japanese game of kemari
📜 Why written rules matter
🇬🇧 What happened in London in 1863
🥅 Why the original 1863 goal had no crossbar
📖 How early football rules differed from today's game

But there is an important distinction: an ancient ballgame is not automatically modern football. The evidence does not establish an unbroken line from ancient games to modern association football. Instead, different cultures developed different forms of ball play, while nineteenth-century England played a crucial role in the codification of modern association football. 

So, did ancient people play football?

The answer depends on what we mean by “football.”

Watch until the end to see how the evidence fits together.
